abstract: INTRODUCTION Altered eating behaviour is a hallmark feature of behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD). These changes may represent a compensatory response to an underlying metabolic disturbance. However, whether increased lipid availability restores metabolic homeostasis or instead accelerates disease progression remains unknown. TDP-43 proteinopathies, which account for approximately half of FTD cases, are associated with alterations in lipid metabolism, providing a mechanistic framework to investigate the cerebral response to lipid overload. METHODS We combined clinical observations in patients with bvFTD with mechanistic studies in the physiological TardbpM323K/M323K knock-in mouse model to determine how TDP-43 dysfunction modifies the response to chronic lipid excess. RESULTS In the bvFTD cohort, elevated cholesterol and triglycerides were associated with poorer cognitive performance, while mutant mice fed a lifelong high-fat diet showed worse cognitive impairment. Multi-omics analyses of the frontal cortex revealed maladaptive metabolic rewiring characterized by impaired mitochondrial and cholesterol metabolism, lipid accumulation, and widespread remodelling of TDP-43-dependent RNA processing. These alterations affected synaptic function and neuronal communication and were accompanied by reduced cerebral glucose utilization measured by 18F-FDG PET, neurotransmitter imbalance and enhanced neuroinflammation. DISCUSSION Increased lipid availability fails to compensate for TDP-43-associated metabolic dysfunction and instead promotes maladaptive molecular and functional responses. These findings identify impaired metabolic resilience as feature of TDP-43-mediated neurodegeneration and suggest that altered eating behaviour in bvFTD may represent an unsuccessful attempt to counteract an underlying metabolic deficit rather than a purely behavioural symptom. Thus, the biological context may determine whether increased energy intake is beneficial or detrimental during neurodegeneration.
